articles.title: An island has been waging war on rats. They think they’ve finally won
articles.summary: Rats are a scourge on island wildlife all over the world. But an island off the coast of Ireland is showing how to successfully gain the upper hand
articles.content:
Rats are a scourge on island wildlife all over the world. But an island off the coast of Ireland is showing how to successfully gain the upper hand

Invasive rats are dangerous predators blickwinkel / Alamy Stock Photo

Thousands of screaming seabirds wheel through the air above and below me as I lean over the railings of a viewing platform halfway down a cliff. The chocolate backs of guillemots are packed so closely on the sheer rock face before me that they seem part of it. Higher up, on precarious ledges, they jostle with fulmars, kittiwakes and puffins, guarding their chicks and waiting for food from their mates.

It’s a wonderful sight, and one that draws in plenty of tourists. But it is not just the birds – much as I love them – that have prompted my trip to Rathlin Island in Northern Ireland. It is another animal that is really responsible for me being here, one that tends to evoke quite different feelings in the human psyche: the rat.

Rats are a huge threat to the seabirds on Rathlin, and the same is true on many islands across the world, where they, and other invasive predators like stoats and cats, eat eggs and chicks. There is now a growing movement for humans to step in and save the birds by killing all the rats. Predator eradication is difficult, but it is “one of the most powerful conservation interventions possible”, says conservation biologist James Russell at the University of Auckland in New Zealand.

Advertisement

Now, the strategy is being applied to Rathlin, one of the largest and most populated islands on which it has been attempted. Success isn’t guaranteed, but it is going well so far, thanks to a campaign involving lethal traps, poison, thermal drones and even a sniffer dog. I have come here to investigate what happens when you try to rid an island of rats, and where the idea goes next.

Rats have a long history of wiping out island birds, with their pawprints all over one of the world’s most famous extinctions, that of the dodo. This unfortunate bird disappeared within 100 years of Dutch sailors arriving on Mauritius, having been hunted by the settlers and their menagerie of pigs, dogs, cats – and stowaway rats.

Whenever rodents arrive on an island with ground-nesting birds that haven’t evolved any defences, they can cause an apocalypse. It is extremely difficult to stop rats from reaching any island that has boat traffic, as they stow away in transported goods, especially animal feed, and can even swim to new islands less than a kilometre away.

Their impact is notorious in New Zealand, whose fauna evolved in geographical isolation for 80 million years, with no rat-like predators – indeed, no native land mammals at all, other than bats. Since humans arrived, the country has suffered sequential invasions of three rat species across its 600-odd islands. The first was in the 13th century, as Polynesian settlers arrived in the north, bringing along Pacific rats.

A few centuries later, these were outcompeted by the larger black and brown rats that hitched rides with European sailors. By the 1960s, conservationists were watching in horror as rodents reached New Zealand’s small outer islands, which until then had been sanctuaries for multiple bird, bat and other native species experiencing precipitous declines on the country’s two main landmasses.

One teacher, Alistair McDonald, took matters into his own hands. In 1960, he was touring Maria Island, a 150-metre-long island off the country’s north coast, when he noticed hundreds of small, delicate-looking seabirds, white-faced storm petrels, floating dead in the water. Rats had finally reached the island.

McDonald turned saving the birds into a school project, encouraging children to fundraise for poisoned rat bait and taking them on hunting expeditions with his dog. Some children even used the more direct method of whacking rats over the head, McDonald told New Zealand Geographic. A park ranger visiting Maria a few years later confirmed the rats were all gone.

McDonald’s school project was one of the first island rodent eradications in the world. Since then, conservationists elsewhere have followed his lead and attempted to eliminate rats and mice from many hundreds of other islands, including those in Australasia, Europe and North America, as well as tropical islands with their unique ecosystems.

Bird populations are easily decimated by predators like rats and ferrets Andy Hay (rspb-images.com)/Cover Images

So far, there have been efforts to eradicate rodents on nearly 1000 islands around the world, with a 90 per cent success rate for rats and 75 per cent for mice (albeit with some reinvasions). Over the years, the techniques have become much more sophisticated. “We started in the 1960s with people crawling around on hands and knees throwing poison everywhere,” says Russell. “Now we use helicopters, sowing the poison aerially. We have gone from islands that were tens of hectares to hundreds of hectares to thousands of hectares.”

Conservationists had been discussing predator eradication on Rathlin Island for more than 20 years. Reports and feasibility studies were partly led by Liz Bell, a New Zealander who is a global leader in the field and who was drawn to Rathlin as the home to Northern Ireland’s largest seabird colony. At about 14 square kilometres, Rathlin isn’t the largest island to undergo predator eradication, but it is the largest one that is fully inhabited.

This is a serious obstacle, as it rules out using helicopters for bait distribution because the poison could be eaten by livestock, pets and possibly even children. “People don’t like poison dropping out of the sky,” says Russell. Instead, the poisoned bait has to go in containers that only rats or smaller creatures can access, which must be placed by hand, massively increasing the work involved.

An added complication was Rathlin’s feral ferret problem. Though there were fewer ferrets than rats, they are lethal predators. In 2017, one ferret managed to reach the cliff-side breeding area I visited, killing 27 puffins over two days.

Despite these difficulties, the idea of eradicating both rats and ferrets on Rathlin gained ground, promoted by conservationists, organisations such as the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) Northern Ireland and some islanders themselves.

The campaigners had to convince farmers and other residents to allow strangers onto their land to distribute lethal traps. But there would be clear benefits. If bird numbers recovered as expected, it would attract more birdwatchers and bring in more tourism, the island’s main source of income. Plus, ferrets and rats are agricultural pests, eating the food of livestock and attacking poultry. After numerous community meetings, several residents joined the campaign as employees or volunteers, and the eradication started in 2023.

A specially trained sniffer dog was brought in to help with the final stages of the rat eradication campaign Anna Feeney/LIFE Raft Project/Cover Images

The first job was to tackle the ferrets. This was done by placing 450 traps around the island, with non-lethal ones used near homes to ensure no pet cats were killed by mistake. In the end, 98 ferrets were killed.

Two years need to have passed since the last sighting for any eradication to be considered certain and, this March, the RSPB proudly announced success – having carried out the first eradication of feral ferrets on an inhabited island in the world.

The rats, however, were a far bigger problem.

With an estimated 10,000 living on Rathlin, it was a mammoth undertaking, requiring 7000 bait stations, designed so nothing larger than a rat could get in and eat the poison. These were placed at 50-metre intervals all over the island. Permission was needed from nearly every resident, as some bait stations had to go in barns, outhouses and even homes.

The farmland and residential areas weren’t the only problematic locations. Much of the shoreline is surrounded by steep cliffs, requiring professional climbers to abseil halfway down and dangle bait stations further down on long wires. “It’s about getting to every last place to make sure that you’ve got total coverage,” says Glenn Slade, project scientist for the RSPB. “If you leave just one pregnant female rat, you’ve potentially got recolonisation.”

The rat poisoning began in September 2024. Slade estimates that most of the rats were killed within the first month. “The vast majority of the decline happens in a short space of time, and then you spend a very long time chasing down those last ones,” he says. That final hunt involved innovative methods like bringing in thermal drones and a specially trained sniffer dog, both of which were used to find any remaining rats.

As far as we know, the last rat was killed in June 2025. So, if all goes well, the campaign could be declared a success by next summer. “I don’t want to jinx it, but, so far, we’ve been successful,” says Slade.

While the intensive part of the campaign is over, several Rathlin residents and volunteers have switched to the monitoring phase, with monthly checks of bait stations and camera traps to ensure no rats remain. They have added extra bait stations and cameras in the harbour area to spot any rats that arrive on boats. If any do, a new localised poisoning campaign would swing into action.

Charlie Bosanquet, a resident who is one of the harbour monitors, says the campaign works only with the islanders’ enthusiastic participation. She helped teach residents to spot signs of rats, giving out laminated sheets with pictures of scat from rats, mice and rabbits, as well as 3D-printed models of rat gnaw marks. The giveaway is that rats have two large front incisors, which leave distinctive grooves. Any resident who notices a rat knows to alert the RSPB.

Life after rats

The residents I speak to enthuse about the benefits of becoming a rat-free island. On my visit, I notice chickens strutting boldly around the lanes and fields, an unusual sight for a Londoner like me. Since rat numbers started falling, some non-farming residents began keeping chickens and ducks, says Marina McMullan, chair of the residents’ group, the Rathlin Development and Community Association.

All those I speak to on the island seem delighted with the campaign apart from one thing: it has led to a surge in rabbits, after the loss of ferrets, their only predators. As I take an evening walk, bunnies certainly bob up and down charmingly through long summer grass, but the next day, I hear how they ravage gardens and farmers’ fields.

I am shown a community allotment near the quay, where a whole row of sunflowers has just been beheaded. Similar destruction has been wrought on the strawberries, peas and herbs. As a keen allotmenteer myself, I feel the pain of this loss.

Then again, this outcome wasn’t wholly unexpected, seeing as the first ferrets were brought to Rathlin by residents in the 1980s specifically to control rabbits. When they got loose and started breeding, it must have felt like the song about the old lady who swallowed a fly.

I ask the RSPB what plans there are for the rabbits. For now, all a spokesperson will say is that their numbers are being monitored. Some of the islanders, however, mutter about taking matters into their own hands.

The rabbits may not seem like a big deal. Farmers elsewhere use various methods to keep their numbers down, including shooting them and gassing their warrens. But they show how, if one species disappears, the effects on an ecosystem’s complex web can be multiple and not always welcome.

When rats are eradicated, there is often a surge in mice, which are usually outcompeted by rats. “My prediction is that mice populations will explode now that the rats are gone,” says Wayne Linklater at California State University in Sacramento, who researches the impacts of invasive species.

Mice are also an agricultural pest and sometimes eat seabird eggs and chicks. On other islands where rats have been eradicated, the surge in mice has been bad news for some other species, like lizards.

When one Rathlin resident wonders aloud to me whether the next step could be eradicating mice, it starts to sound like a game of Whac-A-Mole. Mouse-eradication campaigns are possible, but they are generally harder because the animals are smaller than rats and have even faster breeding cycles.

In the short term, though, there is already an uptick in some seabirds, with about 1700 puffins recorded in 2025 by the RSPB, compared with 1200 in each of the previous two years. There have also been the first signs in decades of breeding by Manx shearwaters and storm petrels.

Rathlin Island seems to now be free of rats and ferrets RSPB

Zooming out, the global picture of rat eradication projects suggests they can have broader benefits than initially expected. On tropical islands, for example, restoring seabirds to their former numbers is thought to also boost coral and its fish, as the birds deposit nutrient-rich droppings. After rat eradication on two Indian Ocean islands in the mid-2000s, seabird numbers steadily rose, and nutrient levels in the surrounding water were found to be 13-fold higher than around similar islands that remained rat-infested.

Just how far could the eradication of introduced predators go? New Zealand is home to Predator Free 2050, a campaign launched by the government in 2016 to rid the entire country of its most harmful invasive predators by the middle of the century. While it first covered rats, possums and stoats, it later expanded to include ferrets, weasels and feral cats. “New Zealand’s ecosystem needs to remove these invasive predators for us to be able to have our seabirds, our land birds and our lizards and frogs back, and our massively cool invertebrates,” says Bell, who advises on aspects of the campaign.

But many conservationists think this goal is both misguided and unachievable. For one thing, it would take huge resources – requiring an estimated NZ$1 billion (US$570 million) a year, more than 0.5 per cent of the country’s GDP – that haven’t yet been made available. And these funds would be better spent in other ways, like protecting islands that are already free of predators, says Linklater, who critiqued the plan while he was based in New Zealand in 2018.

Although it may be unrealistic to eradicate the six invasive predators from the whole of New Zealand, the country has achieved stunning conservation successes through smaller-scale projects on many of its islands, including creating island sanctuaries for birds such as the kakapo, a large, waddling, frankly adorable parrot, and even the iconic kiwi.

Elsewhere in the world, work continues to suppress and eradicate invasive predators, including on both inhabited and uninhabited islands in the Scottish Orkneys and Hebrides.

With so many threats to wildlife from complex global problems like climate change and habitat loss, it is wonderful to work in a field that can count real successes, says Bell. “The recovery of these islands has been mind-blowing in a lot of places,” she says. “Plant recovery, bird recovery, invertebrates, reptiles – it’s magic.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports a successful large-scale conservation effort to eradicate invasive rats and ferrets from Rathlin Island, benefiting native seabird populations and the island ecosystem. The story highlights tangible positive environmental impact with broad significance for island ecosystems globally, supported by detailed context and evidence of ecological recovery.
articles.personality_title: Rathlin Island nears victory in fight to remove invasive rats and ferrets
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Rats and ferrets are invasive predators that harm native wildlife on islands worldwide. They eat eggs and chicks of seabirds, causing serious declines in bird populations. Rathlin Island, off the coast of Northern Ireland, is home to a large seabird colony but has struggled with these pests for years.

**What happened**
In 2023, a large campaign began on Rathlin Island to remove rats and ferrets. The effort used traps, poison bait stations designed only for small pests, thermal drones, and even a trained sniffer dog to find remaining rats. After killing 98 ferrets and an estimated 10,000 rats, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) announced in early 2025 that ferrets were eradicated and rats were likely gone. Local residents helped by monitoring bait stations and looking out for signs of pests.

**Impact**
This is the first time ferrets have been completely removed from a fully inhabited island, and the rat removal effort is one of the largest ever done by hand. Seabird numbers, like puffins, are increasing, and other birds are breeding again after decades. The success shows how communities and conservation groups can work together to protect island wildlife. However, the removal of predators has caused a rise in rabbits, showing how changes in one species affect the whole ecosystem.

**What’s next step**
The islanders and RSPB will continue monitoring to prevent rats from returning. They may also need to manage the growing rabbit population. Some experts predict mice numbers might rise next, which could require further action. Globally, similar projects continue, and New Zealand aims to remove many invasive predators by 2050, though that goal faces challenges.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Rathlin Island’s successful removal of invasive rats and ferrets is helping native seabirds recover and offers a model for protecting island ecosystems worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: L'île de Rathlin proche d'éliminer les rats et les belettes envahissants
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
Les rats et les belettes sont des prédateurs envahissants qui menacent la faune locale sur de nombreuses îles. Ils mangent les œufs et les poussins des oiseaux marins, provoquant un déclin important des populations. L'île de Rathlin, au large de l'Irlande du Nord, abrite une grande colonie d'oiseaux marins mais lutte contre ces nuisibles depuis des années.

**Ce qui s'est passé**
En 2023, une grande campagne a été lancée sur Rathlin pour éliminer les rats et les belettes. L'effort a utilisé des pièges, des stations d'appâts empoisonnés conçues pour les petits animaux, des drones thermiques et même un chien renifleur entraîné pour trouver les derniers rats. Après avoir tué 98 belettes et environ 10 000 rats, la Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) a annoncé début 2025 que les belettes avaient été éradiquées et que les rats avaient probablement disparu. Les habitants ont aidé en surveillant les stations d'appâts et en signalant la présence éventuelle de nuisibles.

**Impact**
C'est la première fois que des belettes sont complètement éliminées d'une île habitée, et la suppression des rats est l'une des plus grandes jamais réalisées manuellement. Le nombre d'oiseaux marins, comme les macareux, augmente, et d'autres oiseaux se reproduisent à nouveau après des décennies. Ce succès montre comment les communautés et les groupes de conservation peuvent travailler ensemble pour protéger la faune insulaire. Cependant, la disparition des prédateurs a provoqué une augmentation des lapins, ce qui montre que les changements d'une espèce affectent tout l'écosystème.

**Prochaine étape**
Les habitants et la RSPB continueront la surveillance pour empêcher le retour des rats. Ils devront aussi gérer la population croissante de lapins. Certains experts prévoient une augmentation des souris, ce qui pourrait nécessiter une nouvelle intervention. Dans le monde, des projets similaires continuent, et la Nouvelle-Zélande vise à éliminer plusieurs prédateurs envahissants d'ici 2050, bien que cet objectif soit difficile.

**Résumé en une phrase**
L'élimination réussie des rats et belettes envahissants sur l'île de Rathlin aide la faune locale à se rétablir et offre un modèle pour protéger les écosystèmes insulaires dans le monde.
articles.personality_title_es: La isla Rathlin cerca de eliminar ratas y hurones invasores
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
Las ratas y los hurones son depredadores invasores que dañan la fauna nativa en muchas islas. Comen huevos y polluelos de aves marinas, causando fuertes caídas en sus poblaciones. La isla Rathlin, frente a la costa de Irlanda del Norte, alberga una gran colonia de aves marinas pero ha tenido problemas con estas plagas durante años.

**Qué pasó**
En 2023 comenzó una gran campaña para eliminar ratas y hurones en Rathlin. Usaron trampas, estaciones de cebo con veneno diseñadas solo para animales pequeños, drones térmicos e incluso un perro entrenado para olfatear las últimas ratas. Tras matar 98 hurones y unas 10,000 ratas, la Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) anunció a principios de 2025 que los hurones fueron erradicados y las ratas probablemente desaparecidas. Los residentes ayudaron monitoreando las estaciones y reportando señales de plagas.

**Impacto**
Es la primera vez que se eliminan hurones completamente de una isla habitada, y la eliminación de ratas es una de las mayores hechas a mano. Las poblaciones de aves marinas, como los frailecillos, están aumentando y otras aves vuelven a reproducirse después de décadas. Este éxito muestra cómo comunidades y grupos de conservación pueden trabajar juntos para proteger la vida silvestre isleña. Sin embargo, la desaparición de depredadores ha causado un aumento de conejos, mostrando cómo los cambios en una especie afectan todo el ecosistema.

**Próximo paso**
Los isleños y la RSPB seguirán monitoreando para evitar que las ratas regresen. También podrían tener que controlar la creciente población de conejos. Algunos expertos predicen un aumento de ratones, lo que podría requerir más acciones. En el mundo, continúan proyectos similares, y Nueva Zelanda busca eliminar varios depredadores invasores para 2050, aunque ese objetivo es difícil.

**Conclusión en una frase**
La exitosa eliminación de ratas y hurones invasores en la isla Rathlin está ayudando a recuperar las aves marinas nativas y ofrece un modelo para proteger ecosistemas isleños en todo el mundo.

articles.title: First mission to fly through monstrous ‘fire clouds’ is about to take off
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02351-5The towering formations appearing over severe wildfires in France and Oregon loft smoke so high they have global consequences.
articles.content:
A giant pyrocumulonimbus cloud formed near the village of Saumos in France last week.Credit: SDIS33/Handout/EPA/Shutterstock

In a hangar in Broomfield, Colorado, a Gulfstream V jet plane is getting last-minute checks before it heads out on a daring mission. The aeroplane is part of a NASA campaign that will, for the first time, extensively sample ‘fire clouds’ — towering, mushroom-like formations that reach into Earth’s upper atmosphere above extremely large and hot wildfires, such as those now burning in France, Spain and the Pacific Northwest.

“We’re seeing these intense fires and unpredictable behaviours,” says Teresa Campos, an atmospheric chemist at the US National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado, who works on the project. “It definitely feels like an important topic to be researching.”

You’re not imagining it: extreme wildfires are now more common

These massive plumes, known as pyrocumulonimbus clouds (pyroCbs), are generated in the hot updraft of the flames and can make their own weather, including winds and lightning strikes that might ignite new fires. PyroCbs also have planetary consequences, lofting smoke into the stratosphere, a layer of Earth’s atmosphere that extends from around 10 to 50 kilometres above the surface. At that altitude, the smoke can spread more readily across the globe, eat away at Earth’s protective ozone layer and influence weather and climate. “We know that they can affect large regions, or even full hemispheres,” says David Peterson, an atmospheric scientist at the US Naval Research Laboratory in Monterey, California, who is the campaign’s principal investigator.

But much about pyroCbs is poorly understood, including how they form, how much smoke they inject into the stratosphere and whether — as many scientists suspect — they are becoming more common as Earth’s climate warms. That’s where the mission, which could see its first flight to fires burning in Oregon as soon as tomorrow, comes in.

So far, scientists have collected only a single sample of fresh smoke in the stratosphere above a pyroCb. All other data come from research planes, flying for other purposes, doing ‘sniff tests’ to measure high-altitude smoke. “This time, it’s going to be more than a sniff,” Peterson says.

INSPYRE’s Gulfstream V sits in a hangar waiting to dive through fire clouds in the coming days.Credit: Alexandra Witze/Nature

Fire chasing

Called the Injected Smoke and Pyrocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE), the campaign aims to get an unparalleled view of fire clouds from the ground up. More than 150 researchers are involved, including scientists at several US universities and staff members at NASA and the US Navy, which is participating because forecasting smoke is important to fly jets.

Air pollution and brain damage: what the science says

The Gulfstream V, which is operated by NCAR, will collect fresh samples of smoke; it has air scrubbers on board to keep things breathable for researchers. Meanwhile, a high-flying jet plane run by NASA will use infrared instruments to scan pyroCbs from above. On the ground, other teams will use technologies such as mobile radars and weather balloons to measure the conditions that fuel the cloud. “It’s effectively fire chasing, the same way you’d go after severe storms,” says Neil Lareau, an atmospheric scientist at the University of Nevada, Reno, who is leading the ground-sensing team.

A group of forecasters will point the fire chasers to where pyroCbs are likely to form. “We’ve been practising all summer” to make better predictions, says Derek Mallia, an atmospheric scientist at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City who is part of the forecasting team. The campaign will run through 10 September, with more field work scheduled next year.

Blowing smoke
articles.reasoning: The article describes a pioneering NASA-led scientific mission to study pyrocumulonimbus clouds formed by extreme wildfires, which have significant global environmental and climate impacts. This research aims to improve understanding of wildfire-related atmospheric phenomena that affect weather, climate, and the ozone layer, potentially informing better forecasting and mitigation strategies. The mission involves extensive collaboration and advanced technology, addressing a critical and growing environmental challenge with broad societal relevance.
articles.personality_title: NASA launches mission to study towering wildfire ‘fire clouds’
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Large wildfires in places like France, Spain, and the US Pacific Northwest create giant clouds called pyrocumulonimbus clouds, or 'fire clouds.' These clouds can reach very high into the atmosphere and affect weather, climate, and even the protective ozone layer.

**What happened** – NASA is sending a special jet plane, a Gulfstream V, from Colorado to fly directly into these fire clouds for the first time. This mission, called INSPYRE, involves over 150 scientists using planes, radars, and weather balloons to study how these clouds form and how much smoke they send high into the sky.

**Impact** – These fire clouds can change weather and spread smoke globally, which may harm the ozone layer and influence climate. Until now, scientists have only had limited data about these clouds. This mission will collect fresh, detailed samples of smoke and measure conditions inside the clouds, helping improve predictions about wildfire effects and air quality.

**What's next step** – The mission will fly over fires in Oregon soon and continue gathering data until September, with plans for more research next year. This ongoing work aims to better understand fire clouds and help communities and pilots prepare for wildfire impacts.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s new mission will provide the first detailed look inside wildfire fire clouds to better understand their effects on weather, climate, and air safety.

articles.personality_title_es: NASA lanza misión para estudiar las enormes ‘nubes de fuego’ de incendios forestales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Grandes incendios en Francia, España y el noroeste del Pacífico en EE. UU. generan enormes nubes llamadas pirocumulonimbos, o ‘nubes de fuego’. Estas nubes suben muy alto en la atmósfera y pueden afectar el clima, el tiempo y la capa de ozono.

**Qué pasó** – NASA está enviando un avión especial, un Gulfstream V, desde Colorado para volar directamente dentro de estas nubes de fuego por primera vez. La misión, llamada INSPYRE, involucra a más de 150 científicos que usan aviones, radares y globos meteorológicos para estudiar cómo se forman estas nubes y cuánto humo lanzan al cielo.

**Impacto** – Estas nubes pueden cambiar el clima y esparcir humo alrededor del mundo, lo que puede dañar la capa de ozono y afectar el clima. Hasta ahora, los datos sobre estas nubes eran limitados. Esta misión recolectará muestras frescas de humo y medirá las condiciones dentro de las nubes para mejorar las predicciones sobre incendios y calidad del aire.

**Próximos pasos** – La misión volará pronto sobre incendios en Oregón y continuará recogiendo datos hasta septiembre, con más investigaciones planeadas para el próximo año. Este trabajo ayudará a entender mejor las nubes de fuego y a preparar mejor a las comunidades y pilotos.

**Resumen en una frase** – La nueva misión de NASA ofrecerá la primera mirada detallada dentro de las nubes de fuego de incendios para entender mejor sus efectos en el clima, el tiempo y la seguridad aérea.

articles.title: Sustainable Personal Care Products for an Earth-Friendly Bathroom
articles.summary:
The average bathroom is a plastic problem hiding in plain sight. Take just one item...
The post Sustainable Personal Care Products for an Earth-Friendly Bathroom appeared first on Earth911.
articles.content:
The average bathroom is a plastic problem hiding in plain sight. Take just one item off the shelf: roughly 20 billion toothpaste tubes are thrown away worldwide every year, and almost none of them are recycled. Multiply that across razors, bottles, floss, and swabs, and a single room quietly generates a steady stream of waste that recycling systems were never built to handle.

Personal care products get bought and tossed on a relentless cycle, and most are built from mixed materials that curbside recycling can’t process. The encouraging news is that durable, refillable, and plastic-free alternatives now exist for nearly every one of them, and for a growing number, independent research backs up the environmental case. Here are options for a lower-waste bathroom, along with what the science does and doesn’t say about each.

This article contains affiliate links. If you purchase an item through one of these links, we receive a small commission that helps fund our work.

Toothpaste Tablets

Toothpaste tubes are among the hardest bathroom items to recycle. Most are sheets of plastic laminate wrapped around a thin layer of aluminum, a fused mix of materials that conventional recycling can’t separate. Globally, that adds up to about 20 billion tubes trashed each year.

The industry has responded. Colgate spent more than five years developing a tube made entirely from #2 HDPE, the same recyclable plastic used for milk jugs, and shared the design with competitors. It began rolling the tube out under its Tom’s of Maine brand around 2019 to 2020 and pledged to convert its full portfolio by the end of 2025, a target it reports it has largely met, with major brands representing roughly 90% of the U.S. market committing to the same switch.

There’s a catch worth knowing: “technically recyclable” is not the same as “accepted curbside.” Few material recovery facilities currently sort toothpaste tubes, and in 2024 a federal judge allowed a consumer lawsuit against Colgate to proceed, alleging its recyclability labeling misleads shoppers whose local programs don’t take the tubes. Check whether your program accepts them before tossing one in the bin.

A simpler way to sidestep the tube entirely is the toothpaste tablet. You chew one until it forms a paste, then brush as usual. Unpaste Zero Waste tablets come in plastic-free, home-compostable pouches and are made without preservatives, dyes, or synthetic fragrances. Early zero-waste toothpastes skipped fluoride, which deterred anyone who wanted the cavity protection dentists recommend; Unpaste now sells both a fluoride and a fluoride-free version.

Biodegradable Dental Floss and the PFAS Question

Floss is a small item with an outsized chemistry problem. Conventional floss is usually nylon or a Teflon-type fiber coated to slide between teeth, and some of those coatings are made with PFAS, the “forever chemicals” that don’t break down in the body or the environment.

In a 2019 study in the Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology, researchers at the Silent Spring Institute and the Public Health Institute measured PFAS in the blood of 178 women and found that those who flossed with Oral-B Glide had higher levels of one PFAS than those who didn’t. It was the first study to link a specific flossing product to a higher body burden of these chemicals. The finding is an association rather than proof of cause, the manufacturer disputed it, and Oral-B has since reformulated Glide to remove PTFE. The lasting lesson: floss doesn’t need PFAS to work, and most flosses tested didn’t contain it.

Lucky Teeth floss avoids the issue on both the health and waste fronts. Its original floss is 100% organic silk coated in candelilla plant wax with tea tree and peppermint oils, fully biodegradable and packaged in a refillable glass jar with paper refill boxes instead of a throwaway plastic dispenser. Silk isn’t vegan, so the company also makes plant-based PLA and bamboo-charcoal flosses in the same refillable glass packaging.

Bamboo Toilet Paper

Toilet paper has a forest problem. Much of the pulp in major U.S. brands comes from the Canadian boreal, the largest intact forest on Earth and one of its most carbon-rich, and the industry clear-cuts more than a million acres of it each year, in part to make a single-use product, according to the Natural Resources Defense Council’s ongoing “Issue with Tissue” reporting. Tissue made from recycled content or responsibly sourced bamboo has roughly one-third the carbon footprint of virgin-fiber tissue, and NRDC lists both as the sustainable alternatives.

Bamboo is a fast-growing grass that regenerates without replanting, which is why it has become a popular tree-free option. We’re big fans of Who Gives A Crap’s bamboo TP, and along with Rizzi Home No. 2 bamboo toilet paper is Forest Stewardship Council and Responsible Forestry certified, wrapped in recycled paper rather than plastic, with soy-ink printed designs. Rizzi also claims to cut down on “butt crumble,” which we’ll let you investigate on your own.

Bamboo Cotton Swabs

Plastic-stemmed cotton swabs are among the most common items found on beaches and in waterways, small enough to slip through filters and reach the ocean. The problem is significant enough that the European Union banned single-use plastic cotton bud sticks in 2021.

The Humble Co. makes a fully biodegradable swab with a handle of sustainably grown bamboo and a cotton tip with natural coloring, packaged in recycled paper. The dentist-founded brand notes its swabs are free of PFAS and BPA, and it funds dental care for underserved communities through its SmileOnU program.

Zero-Waste Shaving

Disposable razors are cheap, ubiquitous, and nearly impossible to recycle: the fused plastic handle, rubber grip, and metal blade can’t easily be separated. The most-cited figure, that Americans throw away about 2 billion disposable razors a year, comes from a 1990 EPA estimate the agency stopped tracking in 2019, so the true number today is unknown and likely higher. What’s clear is that a metal safety razor lasts for years and replaces a steady stream of throwaways.

Albatross reusable metal razors come with 10 replacement blades in a hemp bag. The stainless blades ship in a paper envelope, and the company runs a blade take-back program that accepts used blades from any brand, a genuine fix since most curbside programs won’t take loose razor blades and upcycles the steel into new products. Albatross also makes a shaving soap of plant-based oils in a recyclable metal tin, an alternative to aerosol shaving cream.

Bar Soap

Swapping a pump bottle for a bar is one of the better-studied bathroom trades. In a 2009 life-cycle analysis in Environmental Science & Technology, Swiss researchers Annette Koehler and Caroline Wildbolz found that, per wash, liquid soap carries a carbon footprint about 25% higher than bar soap. Liquid formulas take roughly five times more energy to produce the raw materials and nearly 20 times more energy to make the packaging, and people tend to use about seven times more liquid soap by weight per wash than they do bar soap.

The picture isn’t entirely one-sided. The same study found bar soap has a larger land-use impact, because it relies on farmed vegetable oils, and we tend to use more hot water lathering a bar. But on carbon footprint, packaging, and several toxicity measures, the bar comes out ahead. Look for bars sold unwrapped or in paper; Meow Meow Tweet makes a variety of paper-packed soap bars.

Natural Shampoo Bar

Shampoo doesn’t have to come as liquid in a plastic bottle. Solid bars strip out the water that makes up the bulk of liquid shampoo, which means less packaging and less weight to ship, and they often outlast a bottle.

Meow Meow Tweet makes shampoo bars and powder from organic plant oils and butters with steam-distilled and cold-pressed essential oils and organic botanicals. The bars are package-free and ship in a recycled cardboard box with compostable paper wrapping, labels, and tape, while the powders ship in a recyclable aluminum bottle.

Refillable Body Lotion

Some products just work best as liquids, and lotion is one of them, but you can still cut the plastic with a refillable container. Plaine Products’ body lotion comes in an aluminum bottle with a reusable pump. When you run low, you rinse the empty bottle, mail it back in a refill box, and the company refills and reuses it. The formula is plant-based and vegan, and everything ships in recyclable or compostable packaging.

Bamboo Toothbrush

Every plastic toothbrush ever made still exists somewhere. Americans throw out about a billion of them a year, roughly 50 million pounds of waste, and because the nylon bristles are fused into a polypropylene handle, they can’t go through curbside recycling. They persist for centuries.

A bamboo-handled brush swaps the plastic handle for a compostable one. It’s not a flawless fix, since the nylon bristles still have to be pulled out before the handle can be composted, but the life-cycle research is encouraging. A 2020 assessment in the British Dental Journal, the first to run a full life-cycle analysis on toothbrushes, found that manual bamboo brushes and plastic brushes with replaceable heads had the lowest environmental impact of the options studied, while electric toothbrushes had the highest. The Humble Co., maker of the swabs above, is one dentist-founded brand that makes a bamboo toothbrush.

Menstrual Cups

For anyone who menstruates, disposables add up fast. A person can use around 10,000 pads and tampons in a lifetime, and modern pads are more than 90% plastic that can take centuries to break down. A reusable silicone menstrual cup replaces nearly all that waste and lasts for years.

The environmental case is well supported. A 2021 UN Environment Programme review and a 2022 life-cycle assessment both concluded that reusable menstrual cups have the lowest environmental impact of any menstrual product across their full life cycle, lower than tampons, pads, and even reusable cloth pads and period underwear, which need more water to launder. Cups are the lowest-waste option; reusable cloth pads and period underwear still beat disposables, though by how much depends on how they’re washed.

Where to Take What’s Left After Use

Switching products keeps waste out of the bin, but the items you already own still need somewhere to go. For blades, tubes, and packaging you’re retiring, check what your local program accepts using the Earth911 Recycling Search, and see our guides to recycling toothbrushes and toothpaste tubes and recycling tin and steel cans.

Editor’s Note: Originally published by Jennifer Sokolowsky on July 23, 2019, and updated in July 2026 with current products, links, and supporting research.

articles.title: Roadside milkweed is giving monarchs a new migration highway
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers have planted 9,000 milkweed plants along roads in six North Florida counties, with 6,000 more going in before 2029. Monarchs are already showing up at the sites. The work is part of a national effort led by the University of Illinois Chicago to turn road margins, power line […]
The post Roadside milkweed is giving monarchs a new migration highway first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Researchers have planted 9,000 milkweed plants along roads in six North Florida counties, with 6,000 more going in before 2029. Monarchs are already showing up at the sites.

The work is part of a national effort led by the University of Illinois Chicago to turn road margins, power line easements, and rail corridors into usable habitat for monarchs and other pollinators. Florida’s Department of Transportation joined in 2024, committing to manage 10,200 acres (16 square miles) of roadside land for conservation and awarding a $150,000 grant to the lab of Jaret Daniels, curator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History, to identify, grow, and plant milkweed at sites across the state.

“It’s been a lot of work but also really exciting to see,” Daniels said. “We’ve had good success with plant establishment, and we’ve seen monarchs using the plants already in the field.”

Why roadsides, and why milkweed

Protected land isn’t keeping up with the rate of pollinator habitat loss. But managed land is everywhere. The grass strips beside highways and the margins under power lines get mowed and maintained on a schedule regardless of whether they do anything for wildlife. The question Daniels and his collaborators are testing is whether that work can be redirected.

“We don’t have enough conservation lands to maintain pollinator populations through time in many areas, so we have to look to environments that we, as humans, manage every day,” Daniels said. “Roadsides are managed regardless, so why not do so in a way that confers greater benefits?”

Milkweed is the specific target because of how completely monarchs depend on it. Caterpillars evolved to tolerate the plant’s toxic glycosides by blocking the compounds from binding to cellular receptors, then storing them in their tissue, making the butterflies themselves unpalatable to birds and other predators. The trade-off is absolute: monarch larvae can no longer digest anything else. Milkweed disappears, monarchs disappear with it.

During migration, adult butterflies face a different problem. They can cover more than 100 miles (161 kilometers) a day, which burns through energy fast. Scattered garden patches help, but a continuous corridor of milkweed and wildflowers along a highway gives monarchs a refueling route that matches the scale of the journey.

Other insects feed on milkweed nectar too: bees, moths, wasps, flies, ants. Some get less attention than others. They all show up.

Which plants and why

Daniels’ team evaluated six native milkweed species before settling on two: pinewoods milkweed (Asclepias humistrata) and butterfly weed (Asclepias tuberosa). Both grow naturally in the dry, sandy, low-nutrient soils common along Florida roadsides.

“Both are upland, sand-loving species that would normally be found in pinelands and sandhills,” Daniels said.

Butterfly weed is sold commercially. Pinewoods milkweed is not, so the team builds its own supply. Collectors visit known populations repeatedly during flowering season, tying small bags around developing seed pods to catch the seeds before they drift off on the wind. Those seeds go to the University of Florida Native Plant Nursery, grown in elongated pots that fit the species’ deep taproot. The last batch came in at 98 percent germination.

Planting happens in winter while the plants are dormant, which suits both the plants and field crews who’d rather not be working Florida soil in July. Sites are monitored afterward, and the data on what’s working will shape how the project eventually moves into new counties and other states.

How sites are chosen

Site selection started years before planting. Many of the locations sit adjacent to existing conservation areas. Others are near farms with blueberries and watermelons, crops that depend on wild insect pollination and get a direct benefit from nearby pollinator activity.

An earlier project had already mapped milkweed populations along Florida’s roads, giving the team a starting point. “By partnering with FDOT, we’re trying to fill in gaps where we know appropriate habitat occurs, but there are limited or no milkweeds that grow there,” Daniels said.

The planted areas are now designated wildflower zones, marked with signs. Several are blooming. Monarchs have been seen at multiple sites.
